name: Spinal decompression therapy

lead: Non-surgical spinal decompression uses a computerized table to gently stretch the spine. It is offered mainly for disc herniation and nerve pain, and some posture seekers hope it improves spinal alignment and stature.

The chain is table traction on the spine, eased disc and back discomfort, then more comfortable upright posture. Small randomized trials report pain and disc outcomes in lumbar patients, and some studies measure changes in disc height or herniation size. A 2007 review questioned whether the literature supported efficacy claims in advertising. Appearance outcomes have not been investigated.

paras: Offered by chiropractors and physical therapists, sessions involve lying on a table that applies a controlled stretch, usually repeated over several weeks.
The reviewed sources do not detail adverse effects. Treatment is for back and nerve pain; people with spinal conditions may want to discuss suitability with a clinician.

angle.text: Spinal decompression is offered for disc pain, and some posture seekers hope it improves spinal alignment and stature. The path runs from table traction to eased disc and back discomfort to more comfortable upright posture. Small trials address lumbar pain; appearance outcomes have not been investigated.

lead: Non-surgical spinal decompression therapy is a table-based form of traction, usually computerized, offered by chiropractors and physical therapists for disc herniation and radiculopathy. The term spinal decompression also covers surgeries such as microdiscectomy and laminectomy that relieve pressure on nerves [1].

In looksmaxxing and posture circles it comes up as a way to look after the spine: people who lift, sit for long hours or want a taller, straighter-standing frame treat back comfort and disc health as the base that training, posture work and good carriage are built on. The chain people describe runs from a more comfortable back to training and moving more consistently, and from there to better posture and physique. It is a medical treatment for back and leg pain and is not marketed as a height or appearance procedure.

Small randomized trials report pain, disability and disc outcomes in lumbar patients [2][3][4][5], while a 2007 review questioned whether the literature supported efficacy claims made in advertising [6].

paras: Spinal decompression in general means relief of pressure on the spinal cord or nerve roots. Surgical forms include microdiscectomy, in which part of a herniated disc is removed, and laminectomy, in which part of the posterior vertebral arch is removed to relieve the spinal canal; non-surgical forms include traction and physiotherapy [1]. Compression of a single nerve root produces radiculopathy, named after the root involved, and decompression is a central part of treating radiculopathy, myelopathy and claudication [1].

The non-surgical devices use computerized feedback to deliver segmental distraction to the spine, aiming to relieve pressure on spinal nerve roots [4]. A session typically has the patient lying on a motorized table, harnessed at the pelvis and trunk, while the table cycles through pulling and relaxing phases. Practitioners present the cycling as different from older static traction, and describe it as creating a drop in pressure within the disc.

The treatment is offered for lumbar disc herniation, disc prolapse, radiculopathy and chronic low back pain, usually as part of a package that also includes exercise, electrotherapy or manual therapy [2][4][7]. Clinics also offer cervical versions.

subs.h: Use in looksmaxxing and lifting circles
paras: Strength-training communities discuss disc injuries and their management at length. On T Nation, for example, lifters describe going through physical therapy with spinal decompression after a back injury under heavy squats or deadlifts, with one writer saying it helped with pain relief while questioning whether it actually healed the disc [8]. Others in the same forums describe a mix of approaches, including physical therapy, epidural steroid injections and acupuncture [9][10]. These are personal accounts, not trial data.
No studies found on spinal decompression therapy for appearance outcomes. Trials in lumbar disc patients exist.

A double-blind randomized trial of 20 patients with disc herniation and pain of at least eight weeks gave both groups electrotherapy, deep friction massage and stabilization exercise for fifteen sessions, with one group also receiving decompression. Both groups improved in pain, function and herniation thickness on MRI at three months; herniation shrank more in the decompression group, but the difference between groups was not statistically significant [5].

A study of 30 patients with chronic lumbar pain compared a decompression device with general traction, each given with conservative physical therapy three times a week for four weeks. Both groups improved on pain scores, the Oswestry Disability Index and straight leg raise angle, and the groups did not differ significantly [2]. A comparison of 31 chronic low back pain patients examined joint mobilization with flexion-distraction against decompression therapy on pain and disc height [3].

A 2022 randomized trial of 60 people with lumbar radiculopathy examined adding twelve sessions of decompression over four weeks to routine physical therapy, measuring pain, range of motion, back muscle endurance, disability and quality of life [4]. Another 2022 trial randomized 60 people with subacute herniation to decompression ten times over eight weeks or to a sham in which no force was applied. Leg pain was lower at two months and Oswestry scores lower at two and three months in the decompression group, and MRI showed a larger fall in the herniation index (about 28 percent versus 7 percent) [7].

A single-blind trial of 31 people with chronic disc prolapse compared decompression plus core stabilization exercises with exercises alone; both groups improved significantly, with larger pre-to-post changes in the combined group [11]. A retrospective Cureus study compared motorized traction with non-surgical decompression added to conventional physiotherapy in chronic low back pain from lumbar discopathy [12]. Several Korean physical-therapy studies compared decompression with flexion-distraction or drop techniques on straight leg raise and disc height [13][14].

A 2007 review described the literature as consisting of only one small randomized trial and several lower-level studies at that time, noted that many studies used the VAX-D unit, which places patients prone, while many commercial units use a supine position, and concluded that limited evidence supported routine use given the many less costly alternatives [6]. Wikipedia reports a 2021 meta-analysis that found physiotherapy effective for managing prolapsed lumbar discs without establishing the source of the pain relief, and a finding that mechanical traction decompression was superior to conventional physiotherapy in the short term but not in all studies longer than six months [1].

The trial abstracts summarized here focus on pain, function and imaging outcomes rather than adverse events. Spinal decompression surgeries are a separate category with their own surgical risks [1]. The 2007 review noted that devices had been heavily marketed to manual therapy professions and then to consumers, at equipment prices that could exceed $100,000 [6]. Clinicians generally advise that new or worsening leg weakness, numbness in the saddle area or loss of bladder or bowel control should be assessed urgently, as these are signs of serious nerve compression.

Other non-surgical options for the same conditions include flexion-distraction and drop techniques, manual therapy, core stabilization exercise and vibration traction [3][11][13][15]. A case series of chiropractic multimodal rehabilitation reported radiographic disc height increases after a course of vibration traction [15], and a case report described exercise-based chiropractic management of a firefighter with disc extrusion [16]. Nucleoplasty, a radiofrequency procedure removing nucleus tissue, is a minimally invasive alternative described on Wikipedia [1].
